qti-assessment-test.title: The Medical Letter - Finerenone in T2D CKD & Basal/Concentrated Insulins Review (CME/CPE Demo)

qti-assessment-item.title: Determine the evidence-based starting dose and 4-week potassium titration rule for finerenone in diabetic chronic kidney disease.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Determine the evidence-based starting dose and 4-week potassium titration rule for finerenone in diabetic chronic kidney disease.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A 64-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric CKD takes valsartan 320 mg daily (maximally tolerated) and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily. Baseline labs show eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) 460 mg/g, and serum potassium 4.7 mEq/L. How should finerenone be initiated and monitored?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Start finerenone 20 mg once daily immediately and recheck serum potassium in 6 months.
Start finerenone 10 mg once daily, recheck serum potassium at 4 weeks, and up-titrate to the 20 mg target dose if serum potassium is <=4.8 mEq/L (assuming eGFR has not fallen >30%).
Defer finerenone because concomitant SGLT2 inhibitor therapy is contraindicated and baseline potassium exceeds 4.5 mEq/L.
Add lisinopril 20 mg daily to valsartan before starting finerenone 10 mg twice daily.

qti-content-body.p: Incorrect. The 20 mg starting dose is reserved for baseline eGFR >=60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and delaying potassium monitoring beyond 4 weeks risks undetected hyperkalemia.

Correct. For eGFR 25 to <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and serum K+ <=5.0 mEq/L, finerenone starts at 10 mg once daily; at 4 weeks, increase to 20 mg once daily if K+ is <=4.8 mEq/L, maintain 10 mg if K+ is >4.8 to 5.5 mEq/L, and withhold if K+ >5.5 mEq/L.
Incorrect. Finerenone may be initiated when serum potassium is <=5.0 mEq/L and is routinely co-prescribed alongside SGLT2 inhibitors and a single RAS blocker.
Incorrect. Dual ACE-inhibitor plus ARB blockade is contraindicated due to acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia risk, and finerenone is dosed once daily.

qti-assessment-item.title: Identify contraindicated CYP3A4 metabolic interactions and hyperkalemia hold thresholds during maintenance finerenone therapy.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Identify contraindicated CYP3A4 metabolic interactions and hyperkalemia hold thresholds during maintenance finerenone therapy.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A 59-year-old patient stable on finerenone 20 mg once daily (most recent eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m2, serum potassium 4.9 mEq/L) presents with community-acquired pneumonia, and an urgent-care clinician proposes oral clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily. What prescribing modification is required?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Continue finerenone 20 mg daily alongside clarithromycin because finerenone undergoes exclusively renal tubular secretion.
Double finerenone to 40 mg daily during antibiotic treatment to offset CYP3A4 enzymatic induction.
Co-administer clarithromycin and check serum potassium only if muscle weakness or ECG peaking develops.

Select a non-CYP3A4-inhibiting antibiotic alternative (such as azithromycin or doxycycline when clinically appropriate), because strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like clarithromycin are contraindicated with finerenone due to >4-fold AUC elevation and severe hyperkalemia risk.

qti-content-body.p: Incorrect. Finerenone is primarily cleared via hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 (~90%), not unchanged renal tubular secretion.
Incorrect. Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (not an inducer) and markedly elevates finerenone systemic exposure.
Incorrect. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are strictly contraindicated with finerenone regardless of symptom-triggered monitoring.
Correct. Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, ritonavir, cobicistat) increase finerenone AUC more than 400% and are contraindicated in FDA labeling.

qti-assessment-item.title: Apply comparative basal insulin pharmacokinetics and safe unit-conversion rules when switching from twice-daily NPH to insulin glargine U-300.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Apply comparative basal insulin pharmacokinetics and safe unit-conversion rules when switching from twice-daily NPH to insulin glargine U-300.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A 70-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes on metformin and NPH insulin 30 units twice daily (60 units total daily) experiences two episodes of 3:00 AM symptomatic hypoglycemia (blood glucose 52 mg/dL) despite an HbA1c of 7.6%. To lower nocturnal hypoglycemia risk, the clinician switches basal therapy to once-daily insulin glargine U-300 (Toujeo). Which conversion and titration plan matches FDA labeling?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Initiate insulin glargine U-300 at 48 units once daily (80% of total daily NPH units) using the U-300 prefilled pen without syringe volume math, and titrate no more often than every 3 to 4 days.
Draw 60 units of U-300 glargine out of the pen cartridge using a standard U-100 insulin syringe and inject once nightly.
Start U-300 glargine at 20 units (one-third of total NPH units) because U-300 is three times more potent per unit than U-100 insulin.
Convert unit-for-unit to 60 units once daily and increase by 6 units every 24 hours until fasting glucose is <100 mg/dL.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. When switching from twice-daily NPH to once-daily U-300 glargine, FDA labeling recommends starting at 80% of the prior total daily NPH dose (0.80 x 60 = 48 units) dialed directly in units on the U-300 pen, waiting at least 3 to 4 days between dose adjustments to reach steady state.
Incorrect. Withdrawing concentrated U-300 insulin into a U-100 syringe delivers 3 times the intended insulin dose (180 units) and is strictly prohibited.

Incorrect. One unit of U-300 glargine equals one international unit (though U-300 has slightly lower bioavailability per unit than U-100 glargine); dividing units by 3 confuses volume concentration with unit potency and causes severe hyperglycemia.
Incorrect. Converting twice-daily NPH 1:1 without the 20% reduction and titrating daily before U-300 glargine reaches 3-to-4-day steady state causes insulin stacking and severe hypoglycemia.
